2. Background Art
In a typical telephone network, a first telephone line is typically coupled across a local telephone exchange to transmit an audio signal to one of a series of other interconnected local telephone lines. The relevant local telephone lines are often known as a dialed line or a centerline are connected to a signal detecting device taking the relevant audio reproduction signal and converting it to a digital form according to an assigned digital code.
Alternatively, the relevant line may also be the opposite of the other local lines, such as in a public switched telephone network (PSTN). In such a network, the relevant lines are usually called line associated receive stations and are typically referred to as access lines.
To prevent a reverse party (e.g., a telephone call) being branched to the wrong telephone line, which may have a wrong communicated radio transmission, a reverse party monitoring telecommunications equipment is typically equipped with a transceiver capable of detecting and acting upon telephone calls being made on a subscriber equipment communication line to that subscriber equipment communications circuit. In essence, the transceiver is a communication unit that is located within the telecommunications network. The transceiver typically includes digital circuitry, an antenna and a receiver.
To receive the communications involving the telephone calls to the calling number (or named service number) from the called party irrespective of the location of the calling party's equipment, the telecommunications equipment is typically equipped with two main channels (one for called parties and another for called party calling stations). Andred Mercer (July 7, 1905 – February 8, 1972) was an American architect who designed several buildings in Chicago and New York City.

Biography
Andred Mercer established a successful architectural practice The Des Moines, Iowa architectural firm in 1928, with fellow Iowa architect Samuel McLean.  He was the youngest candidate to become president of the YWCA.

With architectural support from James Christie and Samuel McCardell Mercer, the firm built a house and expanded a hotel on dry five-acre land at 1186 Post Road, in the district of Fulton (Washington County), Westchester County, Illinois, a location from his own initial work. Some of Mercer's more notable buildings included A Boarding House in Riverside, Illinois, a hotel and subway station, a library building, a tavern, and a house for residents.

Mercer was known as one of the townspeople who rejected "great Lippincott" (Lippincott).
